title: Supreme Court Agrees to Hear Trump Immunity Appeal
description_short: The Supreme Court agreed to decide whether Trump has criminal immunity in the federal election interference case.
description_medium: On February 28, 2024, the Supreme Court agreed to hear Trump’s appeal arguing that he had immunity from federal prosecution for actions taken as president. The case arose from the election-interference prosecution over efforts to overturn the 2020 election. Lower courts had rejected his broad immunity claim. The Supreme Court’s review paused the trial while the justices considered the legal question; accepting the appeal did not decide that Trump was immune or resolve the criminal allegations.
description_long: On February 28, 2024, the Supreme Court agreed to hear Donald Trump’s appeal arguing that he was immune from federal prosecution for conduct undertaken as president. The case arose from the federal election-interference prosecution, in which Trump was charged over efforts to overturn the 2020 election result. The trial judge and the federal appeals court had rejected his broad immunity claim, prompting him to ask the justices to intervene. By taking the case, the Supreme Court placed the scope of presidential immunity before the full court and paused the trial while the appeal proceeded. The justices set an expedited schedule and heard argument in April. Accepting review did not decide whether the alleged conduct was official presidential action or whether Trump could be prosecuted. It addressed the threshold legal question that had to be resolved before the criminal case could move forward. The decision therefore affected the timing of the prosecution as well as the law governing presidential accountability. The indictment’s allegations remained allegations, and the Court’s eventual ruling was a separate later development.

title: Facebook Sets Two-Year Suspension for Trump
description_short: Meta said Trump’s suspension would last two years, with reinstatement conditioned on safety assessments.
description_medium: Facebook announced a two-year suspension for Trump on June 4, 2021, replacing the indefinite penalty imposed after January 6. The company acted after its Oversight Board challenged the indefinite suspension and asked it to set a proportionate sanction. Meta said the term ran from January 7 and that reinstatement would depend on a later safety assessment. The announcement set a period, not an automatic return date.
description_long: Facebook announced a two-year suspension for Donald Trump on June 4, 2021, replacing the indefinite suspension imposed after the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. The company acted after its Oversight Board criticized the indefinite penalty and gave Facebook six months to determine a proportionate response. Meta said the suspension would run from January 7, 2021, and that Trump could return only if the risk to public safety had sufficiently receded. The company also said it would assess the seriousness of the risk and consider external factors, including incidents of violence, restrictions on peaceful assembly, and other signs of civil unrest. The decision established a maximum initial period but did not guarantee reinstatement at its end. Facebook said it could extend the suspension if Trump’s conduct continued to pose a serious risk. The case drew attention to how a private platform sets consequences for political speech and to the role of its Oversight Board in reviewing moderation decisions. The announcement concerned access to Facebook and Instagram; it was not a government order restricting Trump’s speech. Whether he would regain access depended on a later review, not simply the passage of two years.
